span.label: exposure-frequency effect (mere exposure)
span.quote: The demonstration of the exposure-frequency effect in the present study is consistent with the findings of Zajonc (1968) and others (e.g., Becknell, Wilson, & Baird, 1963; Johnson, Thomson, & Frinke, 1960).

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Twenty-four female registered nurses at the Hamilton Psychiatric Hospital, Hamilton, Ontario, served as Ss in the present experiment.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Removing one input channel lowers the subject's familiarity with the stimulus, which depresses the rated goodness of its meaning
span.quote: This rating of "goodness," which approaches accepted levels of significance, may be occasioned by S's lower level of familiarity with the stimulus due to the omission of one of the aural sourees of input

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Each of the three input sources (seeing, hearing E, hearing oneself) counts as an exposure, so deleting one cuts effective exposure frequency by a third and should weaken enhancement
span.quote: If one of these three types of exposure were eliminated, Zajonc's hypothesis would predict that S would show less of an enhancement to the stimulus, since he would be deprived of one source of input, reducing frequency of exposure by one-third.

span.label: Far fewer participants were available than in the original studies, one sixth as many per condition.
span.quote: An unexpectedly small number were than in available to the E (12 per eondition), so that only one-sixth as many Ss participated in the present study as did in each of Zajonc's three studies.

span.label: Two of the twelve stimulus words failed to show the effect, which the author attributes to too few subjects.
span.quote: The reason for this may have been an insufficient number of Ss.

span.label: The replication/experimental condition difference did not reach accepted significance levels, again attributed to sample size.

span.quote: Analysis of variance that the indicated exposure-frequency effect was significant (F = 2.72, df = 5/110, p< .025), and that the difference between the replication and experimental approached significance (F = 3.14, df= 1/22, p< .087).

span.label: Collapsing across items, nonsense words seen at high frequencies were rated significantly better in meaning than those seen at low frequencies.
span.quote: An overall t test between the ratings of high- and low-frequency stimulus words the indicated as high-frequency words were significantly "better" (t = 3.34, df= 286, p< .005).

span.label: The effect held at the item level for 10 of the 12 nonsense words, which were rated better at high than at low exposure frequencies.
span.quote: Ten of the 12 stimulus nonsense words were rated as meaning something "better" when they appeared at high-frequency levels (i.e., 5, 10, and 25) than when they appeared at low-frequency levels (i.e., 0, I, and 2).

span.label: Deleting the experimenter's pronunciation did not abolish the mere-exposure effect, showing it can be obtained from nonsense words with one aural input source removed, though overall ratings sat lower on the scale.
span.quote: The results here indicate both that the effect may be obtained with nonsense-word stimuli when E remains silent, and that the effeet tends to appear lower on the "goodness"-of-meaning scale
